children: Australia's corporate regulator said on Wednesday some of the country's pension funds needed to improve scrutiny of their unlisted investments as private markets globally face upheaval.

A new report from the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) found some funds in the country's A$4.8 trillion ($3.34 trillion) pension industry relied too heavily on valuations provided by third-party agencies.
Here are some key points from the ASIC report.

Regulators and investors are keeping a closer eye on private market and unlisted asset valuations following the A$3.4 billion collapse of Sydney homebuilder Bathla and after some private credit funds stopped redemptions recently
ASIC said it reviewed the financial accounts of 42 superannuation funds to examine the valuation and level of information disclosed around their investments

The regulator found the funds often relied on external fund managers to provide valuation information on unlisted investments. That meant the pension funds were limited in their ability to review and challenge valuation assessments and assumptions, ASIC said
Some funds did not adjust their members' liabilities soon enough after a significant write down had occurred, the report found
Information provided by some funds was also not enough for members to understand how some of their investments were valued or the risks that existed around those investments

"We are disappointed and remain concerned about how valuation risks are assessed and addressed for unlisted investments. The persistence of these findings highlights that both superannuation trustees and auditors must take further action," the ASIC report said
The regulator said in September it could take action against "poor practices" by firms in the booming private credit sector, from unrealistic valuations to opaque fees, if standards did not improve
ASIC said it would examine 20 more funds in the current financial year and include 20 managed investment schemes in its review for the first time
